q: I ___ in Jerusalem since I was six.
explain: “Since” + a point in time describes a situation that began in the past and is still true, so we need the present perfect (have lived, or have been living). “I live since…” is a typical Hebrew-speaker error.

q: Your eyes are red. ___ you ___ crying?
explain: The present perfect progressive (have been + -ing) describes a recent activity whose results we can still see now: red eyes.

q: By the time the police arrived, the thieves ___.
explain: The escape happened before the police arrived. For the earlier of two past events we use the past perfect: had + V3.

q: When we reached the cinema, the film ___ already ___, so we missed the beginning.
explain: The film started before we reached the cinema, and the story is told in the past, so we need the past perfect: had already started.

q: If I ___ more free time, I would learn to play the drums.
explain: Second conditional, an unreal present situation: If + past simple, would + base verb. “Would” never appears in the if-clause here.

q: If Shira had left home ten minutes earlier, she ___ the train.
explain: Third conditional, an unreal past: If + past perfect, would have + V3. She didn’t leave earlier, so she missed the train.

q: If I had accepted the job in London last year, I ___ there now.
explain: A mixed conditional: an unreal past condition (had accepted… last year) with a result in the present (now) → would + base verb, here “would be living”.

q: ___ you book tickets soon, there won’t be any seats left.
explain: “Unless” means “if… not”: unless you book soon = if you don’t book soon. With “If”, the sentence would not make sense.

q: The first Dead Sea Scrolls ___ by Bedouin shepherds in the 1940s.
explain: The scrolls didn’t discover anything; shepherds discovered them. A finished past event → past simple passive: were + V3.

q: A new swimming pool ___ near our school at the moment; it should open in the spring.
explain: The pool doesn’t build anything; workers are building it right now → present progressive passive: is being + V3.

q: By the time you read this email tomorrow, the exam results ___.
explain: Future perfect passive (will have been + V3): an action that someone will complete before a point in the future. The results are published by someone, so the verb is passive.

q: “Don’t touch the paintings,” the guide told us. → The guide told us ___.
options: that we don’t touch the paintings
explain: A reported command: tell someone (not) to + base verb. “Don’t touch” → told us not to touch.

q: “Have you ever been to Japan?” Yoav asked me. → Yoav asked me ___.
options: if I had ever been to Japan
if had I ever been to Japan
had I ever been to Japan
that had I ever been to Japan
explain: A reported yes/no question uses if/whether + statement word order (subject before verb), and the tense moves back: have been → had been.

q: The lights are off and nobody is answering the door. They ___ out.
explain: The evidence makes us almost sure, so we use “must be”. “Can’t be” would mean we are sure they are not out. In deduction, the opposite of “must” is “can’t”.

q: You ___ my sister at the party on Friday. She was in Eilat all weekend.
explain: We are sure something did not happen in the past → can’t have + V3. She was in Eilat, so you can’t have seen her at the party.

q: The girl ___ painting won the competition is in my class.
explain: “Whose” shows possession: the girl’s painting → the girl whose painting. “Who’s” is short for “who is”.

q: Which sentence is correct?
options: My grandmother, who was born in Morocco, speaks four languages.
My grandmother, that was born in Morocco, speaks four languages.
My grandmother, who she was born in Morocco, speaks four languages.
My grandmother, which was born in Morocco, speaks four languages.
explain: In a non-defining clause (between commas) we use who or which, never “that”; for a person, who. Don’t repeat the subject: “who she was” copies the Hebrew “שהיא”.

q: I’m really looking forward to ___ you at the reunion.
explain: In “look forward to”, “to” is a preposition, so a gerund follows it: looking forward to seeing you. The same is true of “used to” in “I’m used to waking up early”.

q: Hila stopped ___ coffee in the evening because it kept her awake at night.
explain: Stop + -ing = quit a habit. Stop + to-infinitive = pause in order to do something else. Coffee kept her awake, so she quit: she stopped drinking it.

q: Our room was small and quite noisy. ___, the view from the balcony was breathtaking.
explain: “However” starts a new sentence that contrasts with the one before, and is followed by a comma. “Although” and “despite” join two parts of one sentence.

q: ___ the heavy traffic, we arrived at the airport on time.
explain: “Despite” is followed by a noun phrase: despite the heavy traffic. “Although” and “even though” need a full clause: although the traffic was heavy.

q: Tamar loves big, noisy parties, ___ her twin sister prefers quiet evenings at home.
explain: “Whereas” contrasts two different facts in one sentence: one sister likes this, whereas the other likes that.

q: In the sentence “Adi was reluctant to share her poems, afraid that people would laugh at them,” what does “reluctant” mean?
explain: Reluctant = not wanting to do something; unwilling. Her fear of being laughed at explains it. “Eager” is the opposite, and she is able to share them, just not willing.

q: “After the storm, the streets were eerily silent.” What does “eerily” suggest?
options: In a strange way that feels frightening
In a calm and pleasant way
In a loud and noisy way
In a sad but beautiful way
explain: Eerie means strange and slightly frightening, because something feels unnatural. An eerie silence makes you uneasy.

q: Critics described the ending of the film as “ambiguous”. This means the ending ___.
options: could be understood in more than one way
explain: Ambiguous = open to more than one interpretation; viewers can’t be sure what really happened.

q: Despite decades of ___, the two countries finally signed a peace agreement.
explain: “Despite” signals a contrast with the peace agreement, so we need a negative word: hostility (unfriendliness and conflict). Don’t confuse it with hospitality, welcoming guests.

q: What does “acquire” mean?
explain: Acquire = to get or gain: acquire a skill, acquire knowledge. Don’t confuse it with require (לדרוש) or aspire (לשאוף).

q: What does “gradually” mean?
explain: Gradually = slowly, step by step: The pain gradually disappeared. Its opposite is suddenly (בפתאומיות).

q: What does “inevitable” mean?
explain: Inevitable = certain to happen; it can’t be avoided: Some change is inevitable. Don’t confuse it with unpredictable (בלתי צפוי).

q: “She glanced at the clock and kept writing.” To glance is to ___.
explain: A glance is a quick look. Compare: stare = look for a long time; glare = look angrily.

q: “By midnight, the town square was deserted.” This means that ___.
explain: Deserted = empty, because everyone has left. It comes from the verb “desert” (to leave or abandon), not from the desert as a place.

q: Take your time: you don’t have to ___ a decision today.
explain: The collocation is “make a decision”. Others with make: make a mistake, make progress, make an effort.

q: Please ___ attention to the safety instructions before the flight.
explain: In English we “pay attention” to something (לשים לב). Do, make and take don’t combine with “attention” this way.

q: The campaign aims to ___ awareness of plastic pollution in the sea.
explain: We “raise awareness”, i.e. make more people know about an issue. “Raise” takes an object; “rise” and “arise” don’t: prices rise, but shops raise prices.

q: After studying the data for weeks, the researchers were finally able to ___ a conclusion.
explain: We “draw a conclusion” (or reach / come to one). “Make up” means invent.

q: When you choose a university, ___ in mind that the cost of living differs from city to city.
explain: “Bear in mind” = remember and take into account. (“Keep in mind” means the same, but hold, put and take are not used this way.)

q: Regular exercise is ___ to both your body and your mood.
explain: After “is” we need an adjective: beneficial (good for, helpful). Benefit is a noun or verb; beneficially is an adverb.

q: The coach’s ___ to let injured players train surprised no one.
explain: After a possessive (the coach’s) we need a noun: refusal. Refuse is the verb.

q: Which word is the opposite of “responsible”?
explain: Many adjectives beginning with r take the prefix ir-: irresponsible, irregular, irrelevant. Compare il- (illegal) and im- (impossible).

q: Sorry, I ___ you. I thought you said Tuesday, not Thursday.
explain: The prefix mis- means “wrongly”: misunderstand, misspell, mislead.

q: We lost 5–0 because we ___ the other team; we thought they would be easy to beat.
explain: Under- = too little: to underestimate someone is to think they are weaker than they really are. Over- = too much: overestimate.

q: She spoke so ___ about animal rights that the whole audience was moved.
explain: “Spoke” is a verb, and a verb is described by an adverb: passionately. Passion is the noun, passionate the adjective.

q: Read: “Many teenagers sleep with their phones next to their beds. Experts warn that this habit can make it harder to fall asleep.” What does “this habit” refer to?
options: Keeping a phone next to the bed at night
Switching the phone off at night
explain: “This habit” points back to the previous sentence: sleeping with the phone next to the bed.

q: Read: “Join our beach clean-up this Friday at 9:00! Bring gloves, a hat and a friend. Last month, forty volunteers collected over 200 kilos of plastic. Let’s beat that record!” What is the main purpose of this text?
options: To persuade people to take part in an event
To warn people about the dangers of the sun
To complain about people who pollute beaches
To report the results of a competition
explain: The imperatives (Join! Bring!) and the call to “beat that record” show that the writer wants readers to come and volunteer. Last month’s result only supports that aim.

q: Read: “Oh, wonderful. The bus is late again, it’s pouring with rain, and my umbrella is at home. What a perfect start to the day.” The writer’s tone is ___.
explain: The writer says “wonderful” and “perfect” but describes only bad things. Saying the opposite of what you mean is sarcasm.

q: Read: “When the results were posted, Yarden read the list twice. Then she quietly closed her laptop, put on her running shoes and went out without a word.” What can we infer?
options: Yarden was probably disappointed with her result.
Yarden got the highest grade in the class.
Yarden was late for a race.
explain: Reading the list twice, closing the laptop quietly and leaving without a word suggest she didn’t find what she had hoped for. Nothing in the text supports the other options.

q: Read: “The museum opened in 1965 and has over 500,000 objects in its collection. It is, without doubt, the most fascinating place in the city.” Which of these is an opinion, not a fact?
options: It is the most fascinating place in the city.
explain: Dates and numbers can be checked, so they are facts. “The most fascinating” is a personal view, so it is an opinion, even with “without doubt”.

q: Read: “Social media companies claim they care about young users. Yet their apps are designed to keep teenagers scrolling for as long as possible, often late into the night.” What is the writer’s attitude towards these companies?
explain: “Claim” suggests the writer doubts what the companies say, and “Yet” introduces evidence against it. The writer is critical.

q: Read: “The opening night was a disaster: the lights failed, an actor forgot his lines and the curtain got stuck. Still, the director smiled. ‘Well,’ she said, ‘the only way is up.’” What does the director mean?
options: Things can only get better from now on.
The actors should stand higher on the stage.
The curtain must be raised again.
explain: After everything went wrong, things can’t get any worse, so they can only improve. “Still” shows that she stays positive.

q: Read: “For centuries, people believed that the Sun moved around the Earth. The idea seemed obvious: anyone could watch the Sun rise and set. However, a few astronomers began to notice problems with this view.” What will the next paragraph most likely discuss?
options: The evidence that challenged the old belief
How to watch a sunset safely
Why the old belief was correct
The daily lives of ancient farmers
explain: “However” and “problems with this view” prepare the reader for evidence against the old belief.

q: Read: “Grandpa never talked about the war. But every year, on one particular day in April, he would take out an old photograph, look at it for a long time, and put it away without a word.” What can be inferred?
options: The photograph is connected to painful memories.
Grandpa forgets about the war every April.
The photograph was taken last April.
explain: His silence about the war and his silent yearly ritual suggest the photograph reminds him of something painful from that time. Nothing supports the other options.

q: Read: “Learning a musical instrument does more than produce music. Studies suggest that it improves memory, teaches patience and even helps students concentrate in class.” What is the main idea?
options: Playing an instrument has benefits beyond music.
Music is more important than other school subjects.
Only children should learn to play instruments.
Learning an instrument is very difficult.
explain: The first sentence states the main idea, and the second gives examples of benefits beyond the music itself.

q: Read: “Some people see graffiti as vandalism. Others see it as art that belongs to everyone. In some cities, artists are now paid to paint walls that were once covered in illegal tags.” Why does the writer mention the paid artists?
options: To show that attitudes towards graffiti are changing
To prove that graffiti is always illegal
To complain about the cost of public art
To explain how to become a street artist
explain: Walls once covered in illegal tags are now painted by paid artists: an example of how some cities have come to see graffiti as art.

q: Read: “The mountain path was so treacherous after the storm that the guide made everyone hold the rope. Even so, two hikers slipped.” In this text, “treacherous” means ___.
explain: The rope and the hikers slipping are clues: the path was dangerous. (“Treacherous” can also mean disloyal, but not here.)

q: Read: “The old cinema on Herzl Street is a phone shop now. I still remember the smell of popcorn, the red velvet seats, and the hush when the lights went down.” The writer’s tone is best described as ___.
explain: The writer remembers the past fondly, with some sadness that it is gone. That feeling is nostalgia.

q: Read: “In the experiment, half the students studied with music in the background and half studied in silence. The silent group remembered more words, but both groups said they enjoyed the session.” Which statement is supported by the text?
options: The silent group remembered more words than the music group.
The music group enjoyed the session more.
Music made the students lose interest.
Both groups remembered the same number of words.
explain: The text says the silent group remembered more words. Both groups enjoyed the session, so we can’t say one enjoyed it more or lost interest.

q: Read: “The school banned phones during breaks. ‘Finally, students will talk to each other,’ the principal said. The students have indeed found a new hobby: complaining about the ban, together, face to face.” What is ironic here?
options: By complaining together, the students are doing exactly what the ban was meant to achieve.
The students are using their phones to complain.
The principal has changed his mind about the ban.
The students have stopped talking to each other.
explain: The irony: the students oppose the rule, yet their protest, talking face to face, is the very result the principal wanted.

q: Read: “Electric scooters are cheap, quick and good for the environment. On the other hand, they cause hundreds of injuries every year, and many riders ignore traffic laws.” What is the writer doing in this text?
options: Explaining how to ride a scooter
Persuading readers to buy a scooter
explain: The first sentence lists advantages; “On the other hand” introduces the disadvantages.

q: Read: “By the time Ella reached the stage, her hands had stopped shaking. She looked at the crowd, found her mother’s face in the third row, and began to sing.” How did Ella probably feel before she reached the stage?
explain: Her hands “had stopped shaking” by the time she reached the stage, so before that they were shaking: she was nervous.

q: Read: “The city planted 500 trees last year. Environmental groups welcomed the move but called it ‘a drop in the ocean’ compared with the thousands of trees cut down.” What do the groups mean?
options: It is far too little to make a real difference.
The trees were planted too close to the sea.
It was a waste of water.
explain: “A drop in the ocean” is a tiny amount compared with what is needed. “Welcomed… but” shows they liked the move yet thought it was not nearly enough.

q: Look outside! It ___ . Don’t forget your umbrella.
explain: “Look!” shows it is happening now, so we use the present progressive: am / is / are + verb-ing. “Raining” alone is missing “is”.

q: My brother ___ to the gym three times a week.
explain: “Three times a week” is a habit, so we use the present simple. With he / she / it we add -s (or -es): goes.

q: Water ___ at 100 degrees Celsius.
explain: A scientific fact that is always true takes the present simple.

q: Shh! The baby ___ . Please don’t wake her up.
explain: “Shh!” tells us it is happening right now: present progressive.

q: ___ your sister ___ in Haifa?
explain: Present simple questions with he / she / it: Does + subject + base verb. The -s moves to “does”, so “live” has no -s.

q: She ___ coffee. She prefers tea.
explain: A general preference, not something happening now: present simple. Negative with she: doesn’t + base verb (no -s).

q: How often ___ your grandparents?
explain: “How often” asks about a habit: present simple. Question with you: do + subject + base verb.

q: ‘What ___ for a living?’ ‘She’s a nurse.’
explain: A job is a permanent situation: present simple. Question: does + subject + base verb (do, not does).

q: I ___ to music while I study. It helps me concentrate.
explain: A habit (usually) takes the present simple. Adverbs of frequency go before the main verb: I usually listen.

q: ‘Can I borrow your laptop?’ ‘Sorry, I ___ it at the moment.’
explain: “At the moment” means right now: present progressive (I’m using).

q: My dad ___ from home this week because his office is being painted.
explain: “This week” describes a temporary situation, so we use the present progressive, even though it isn’t happening this very second.

q: Maya usually takes the bus to school, but this week she ___ her bike because the bus drivers are on strike.
explain: The usual habit is in the present simple (usually takes); the temporary change this week is in the present progressive (is riding).

q: ‘What are you doing tonight?’ ‘I ___ my cousins at the mall at eight. We arranged it yesterday.’
explain: The present progressive also describes future plans that are already arranged (a time and place are fixed).

q: According to the timetable, the last bus ___ at 23:40 every night.
explain: Timetables and schedules (“every night”, “according to the timetable”) take the present simple.

q: The climate ___ , and summers in Israel are getting hotter.
explain: A situation that is developing now, a trend, takes the present progressive. “The climate” is singular, so “is”, not “are”.

q: I ___ what you mean, but I don’t agree.
explain: “Understand” is a stative verb (a state of mind, not an action), so it is not normally used in the progressive.

q: This soup ___ delicious. What’s in it?
explain: “Taste” as a quality of the soup (how it seems) is stative: present simple.

q: The chef ___ the soup to see if it needs more salt.
explain: Here “taste” is an action the chef is doing right now (he is trying it), so it can be progressive.

q: Dana ___ two cats and a dog.
explain: “Have” meaning own / possess is stative: present simple, with -s for she: has.

q: We ___ a great time in Eilat! The weather is perfect.
explain: “Have a great time” is an experience, not possession, so “have” can be progressive here: we’re having.

q: Choose the correct spelling: The kids are ___ in the pool.
explain: One-syllable verbs ending consonant-vowel-consonant double the last letter before -ing: swim → swimming (also run → running, sit → sitting).

q: Choose the correct spelling: The cat is ___ on the sofa.
explain: Verbs ending in -ie change -ie to -y before -ing: lie → lying, die → dying, tie → tying.

q: Which time expression usually goes with the present progressive?
explain: Now, right now, at the moment, currently, this week: present progressive. Every day, usually, on Sundays: present simple.

q: Which time expression usually goes with the present simple?
explain: Habits and routines (once a week, always, never, every morning) take the present simple.

q: He ___ always ___ his phone in class! It drives the teacher crazy.
explain: “Always” with the present progressive expresses annoyance at a habit that keeps happening: He is always checking his phone!

q: Which sentence is NOT correct?
options: This bag is belonging to my sister.
I don’t need any help, thanks.
We’re seeing the dentist on Monday.
explain: “Belong” is stative, so “This bag belongs to my sister”. “We’re seeing the dentist on Monday” is fine: “see” here means meet, an arranged plan.

q: Only one of these sentences is correct. Which one?
options: I’m thinking of quitting the team.
I’m thinking that the plan is good.
I am wanting a new phone.
explain: “Think of / about” (considering) is an activity and can be progressive. “Think that” (an opinion), “know” and “want” are stative: I think that…, she knows, I want.

q: Which question is correct?
options: Do you know where the station is?
Are you knowing where the station is?
Does you know where is the station?
You know where is the station?
explain: “Know” is stative: Do you know…? Inside the question, “where the station is” keeps the order of a statement (subject before verb).

q: I ___ this song! Who sings it?
explain: “Love” is a stative verb (a feeling), so the present simple is correct. Slogans like “I’m loving it” are informal exceptions.

q: Which sentence describes a temporary situation?
options: I’m staying with my aunt until our flat is ready.
explain: The present progressive (I’m staying… until…) shows the situation is temporary. The others are permanent facts or schedules in the present simple.

q: Read: “Our school’s robotics team meets every Tuesday after school. At the moment, the team is building a robot that can sort recycling, and it is hoping to enter the national competition in March.” What is the team doing now?
options: Building a robot that sorts recycling
explain: “At the moment, the team is building…” tells us what is happening now. The competition is in March, and they meet only on Tuesdays.

q: Read: “More and more teenagers are choosing to work part-time while they are still at school. Some are saving for a car; others enjoy the independence. Teachers worry that long shifts leave students too tired to study.” What is the text mainly about?
options: Teenagers who work while they are at school
How to save money for a car
The best part-time jobs for students
explain: Every sentence is about school students with part-time jobs: why they work and what teachers think. A car is only one example.

q: Read: “The library is introducing a new rule: from next month, visitors can borrow up to ten books at a time. Until now, it allowed only five.” What does “it” refer to?
explain: Until now, the library allowed only five books. “It” points back to the subject of the first sentence.

q: Read: “Shira is standing at the bus stop, checking her watch every few seconds. She keeps looking down the road and sighing loudly.” How does Shira probably feel?
explain: Checking her watch again and again, looking down the road and sighing: she is waiting and wants the bus to come now.

q: Read: “Are you tired of waiting in long lines? Download the FastPass app today and order your coffee before you even reach the café. Your first drink is free!” What is the purpose of this text?
options: To explain how coffee is made
To warn people about long lines
explain: The imperative (Download!) and the free first drink are typical of an advertisement: it wants you to get the app.

q: Read: “I can’t believe it. I’ve waited six months for this concert, and now they’re cancelling it two hours before the show, with no explanation and no refund!” The writer’s tone is ___.
explain: “I can’t believe it”, the long wait, no explanation, no refund and the exclamation mark all show anger.

q: Read: “The town is famous for its annual festival. Each summer, thousands of visitors arrive for the music, the food and the fireworks.” In this text, “annual” means ___.
explain: “Each summer” is the clue: the festival takes place once every year.

q: Read: “Doctors are warning parents about energy drinks. These drinks contain large amounts of caffeine and sugar, and they are becoming popular among children as young as ten.” What does “they” refer to?
explain: The drinks are what contain caffeine and are becoming popular; “they” continues “these drinks”.

q: Read: “Ido opens the fridge and closes it, then opens the cupboard and closes that too. Then he picks up his phone and starts looking for the number of the pizza place.” What can we infer?
options: He doesn’t find anything he wants to eat at home.
He works at a pizza place.
explain: He searches the fridge and the cupboard, finds nothing he wants, and turns to ordering pizza.

q: Read: “The plant is thriving in its new spot by the window: it is growing new leaves almost every day, and its flowers are bigger than ever.” In this text, “thriving” means ___.
explain: The words after the colon explain it: new leaves every day and bigger flowers. The plant is doing very well.

q: Read: “The new stadium holds 30,000 people, and its roof opens in two minutes. It is the most beautiful building in the country.” Which of these is a fact from the text?
options: The roof opens in two minutes.
It is the most beautiful building in the country.
The stadium is too big for the city.
explain: A number that can be checked is a fact. “The most beautiful” is an opinion, and the last two are not in the text at all.

q: Read: “Every evening, Mr. Levi waters his neighbour’s garden and collects her mail. This month he is also feeding her cat, and he leaves her porch light on at night.” What can we infer about the neighbour?
options: She is afraid of the dark.
explain: Someone else collects her mail, feeds her cat and leaves a light on for her: things people arrange when they are away.

q: Read: “Scientists are studying a small fish that can survive in water hotter than 40°C, a temperature at which most fish die. They hope it will help them understand how animals may adapt to warmer oceans.” Why are the scientists studying the fish?
options: To learn how animals might cope with warmer seas
To find a new kind of food
To prove that most fish like warm water
To protect the fish from extinction
explain: The last sentence gives the reason: they hope the fish will show how animals may adapt to warmer oceans.

q: Read: “Many people believe multitasking saves time. In fact, each time we switch tasks, the brain needs a moment to refocus. As a result, doing two things at once often takes longer than doing them one after the other.” What is the writer’s main point?
options: Multitasking is often less efficient than people think.
Our brains work faster when we multitask.
Research about the brain is usually wrong.
People should do only one task a day.
explain: “In fact” corrects the common belief, and “As a result” gives the conclusion: multitasking often takes longer.

q: Read: “Noam usually works at the café on weekends, but this month he is working there every evening, because one of the waiters is on holiday.” Which statement is true?
options: Noam is working more than usual this month.
Noam works at the café every evening all year.
Noam is on holiday this month.
explain: Usually (present simple) he works only on weekends; this month (present progressive) he is also working every evening, so he works more.

q: Read: “For years, the island’s coral reefs were dying. Then local fishermen agreed to stop fishing in part of the bay. Today, divers report that the reefs are slowly recovering and fish are returning.” What does the text suggest?
options: Protecting part of the bay helped the reefs recover.
Fishermen are destroying the reefs today.
Divers caused the reefs to die.
The fish have left the island forever.
explain: The order of events, reefs dying, fishing stopped, reefs recovering, suggests the protection is the reason.

q: Read: “Bees are disappearing in many parts of the world. This is not only a problem for bees: about one third of the food we eat depends on plants that bees pollinate.” Why does the writer mention the food we eat?
options: To show why the bees’ disappearance matters to people
To explain how bees make honey
To suggest that people should eat less
explain: “Not only a problem for bees” prepares us for why it matters to us too: much of our food depends on them.

q: Read: “Every Friday morning, hundreds of volunteers deliver food to elderly people who live alone. For many of them, the visit is the only conversation they have all week.” Which is the best title?
options: How to Cook for a Crowd
Why Old People Don’t Like Visitors
explain: The text says the visit gives the elderly company as well as food, so the visit is more than a meal.

q: Read: “The company says it is ‘going green’. Yet it is still flying its managers to meetings that could easily take place online, and its factories are burning more coal than ever.” What does the writer suggest?
options: The company’s green claims are hard to believe.
The company is the greenest in its industry.
Online meetings are bad for the environment.
explain: “Says” and the quotation marks show doubt, and “Yet” introduces facts that contradict the claim.

q: Read: “Tal was going to apologise, but at the last minute she got cold feet and said nothing.” What does “got cold feet” mean here?
options: became too nervous to do it
forgot what she wanted to say
explain: She planned to apologise but, at the last minute, did nothing: “get cold feet” means to lose your courage before doing something.
